It's surprising to me, that some people need everything to be for them. None of them considered, that maybe they might not be the target audience. It's not like Sigma has some kind of monopoly, where the consumer is hurt by them not innovating or something. It is a camera for the smartphone person that wants something, that is also everyday good looking and doesn't know anything about cameras. 
For example the internal storage. I get why they did it. Like, how many different SD card standards are there. I used to work in tech support, most people will turn of their monitor if you ask them to turn of the computer with the button. Just choosing the sd card is probably already quite a hurdle for them. And that is ok, they might know how to repair a shoe, make Excel sheets that I couldn't understand even if I sit there for hours or know exactly what the problem is, when you are hurt and can't even explain what part of your own body is hurting. Not everybody needs to be good or invested in everything.
This camera is not for professionals or nerds like me, so why hate it, for something that it's not even trying to be.

Author: @drustill
Content:
Before the throng of photogs crucify the OEM for excluding what they deem to be "table-stakes" for a pro-grade camera, take a second to reread the headline. This is about as much of a professional photography tool as your iPhone—albeit one that's a bit more dedicated, featuring certain capabilities and hardware not typically found in the device living in your pocket—like an actual optical lens.

The size is a bit questionable when we zero in on the likely target market: the 18-to-30-something hipster photogs more concerned with capturing sunsets on weekend getaways or snapping their meticulously layered matcha at the local artisan café. That said, this group is never without a shoulder bag or backpack, so let’s hope the ergonomics don’t clash with the carry setups common to that crowd.

At the end of the day, the best camera is the one you have with you. And if you don’t have it with you, it’s just a really expensive—but admittedly cool—paperweight.

Author: @Seanvandeusen
Content:
Sigma got it right the FP and LP. They ignored RED and still delivered CDNG video files. The camera is practically a pocket size Arri. 

However, a lot of people bought it for photos and fell in love with their color science.. rightfully so. The photos I got out of mine are up there with the XH2S and Leica. For some, that alone can be a deal breaker because it’s hard to get more natural colors which Canon and Nikon offer via Standard or Portrait modes. 

But for street photography your colors pop with Sigma cameras. This camera is the result of Sigma listening to their consumers. Rather than hyper focus on video… they main a camera more so focused on photos while keeping the same body shape, size and overall form factor. Pair this with a 27mm pancake lens and it literally fits in your pocket. Sigma’s colors pop in places like Vegas, NYC and Puerto Rico. I’m typically not someone who shoots jpegs because I love editing… but with this camera you can shoot either or and I can assure you’ll be happy with the results straight out of the camera. Fuji owners would appreciate this. 

Without a flash, external storage and I believe it uses an electric shutter like its previous cameras… this isn’t for pro work but as a professional photography I can promise you you’ll grab it for traveling and a day out at the beach. 

The downside in my opinion is the storage and price. I rather not have this sitting on my desk transferring files or relying on WiFi to transfer files. If I want to check out and edit my files I rather pop out an SD card in and out of the camera and my laptop. And at that price point you’re better off getting a Fuji XT5 or XT50 (compact). Partied with a pancake lens for travel and street photography you’ll get the same compact design but you also get a viewfinder, sd card slot, mechanical and electric shutter, a hotshoe for flash and triggers and it can hook up to external monitors with ProRes Raw and Braw recording capabilities if you’re a video shooter.

Content:
The rear display is a viewfinder. 
It is not a "eye-level viewfinder" because you do not place eye in it.

And it is not "waist-level viewfinder" as it is not a tilt screen, that you could look it from above.

And it is not a "wire-frame viewfinder" aka "sports viewfinder" as you don't have a hotshoe where to attach one.

But one could make an argument that fixed rear LCD is a eye-level viewfinder as you hold it on eye-level, but it is same time like a sports-viewfinder that you keep it at about arms length.

Content: 230gb can get full quick if you take multiple 4k pictures at once. Not being able to easily swap out the SD card is highly impractical and also disrupts the workflow. So in the scenario of a full day of shooting, you’d also have to carry around a laptop that you could connect the camera too and offload all the pictures onto. And if you laptop doesn’t have a lot of internal storage, you need to offload pictures onto a cloud, and if you’re shooting somewhere where you don’t have access to good internet signal you’d need to carry around external SSD's. This is not for serious professionals. This is more for the casual person who wants to document their city trips, but for that purpose the camera in modern day phones is usually more than enough.

Author: @amalkatrazz
Content:
It’s Sigma BS. Weird that a respectable manufacturer would come with such an atrocity. Not a single photographer worth his Lightroom preset collection would consider this for a main camera or even a travel camera.

- Ergonomics isn’t there. It might be lightweight but a solid uniform brick is harsh to hold for extended periods of time.
- Control isn’t there. Even budget m43 lumix cameras have 4 dials and 10-12 programmable buttons so you could quickly change the important settings for each shot.
- Longevity isn’t there. SSDs aren’t famous for surviving constant rewrite. A professionally used camera fills up 256 gigs in a matter of days.
- Ease of use isn’t there. SD cards are the bread and butter for a good reason. You pop the card out, put it into your computer and get the files out. You don’t need to carry an extra cable for that. Doesn’t seem to be the case here.
- Ewaste is there. Nonremovable battery? So you need to charge between uses instead of just taking the battery out and inserting a precharged spare? How convenient! And what to do when the battery’s capacity inevitable goes down? Throw the whole unit away?

I don’t know who this device is for. Its many dubious design flaws make it unsuitable for professional photography. Its premium price makes it unsuitable for any other sort of photography.

Author: @roscot40
Content:
I keep on hearing, “if Apple made a camera…” and as much as I dislike the tech giant.  That simply isn’t the case here.

The Sigma BF adopts some of the stylistic choices Apple have already used in their manufacturing and the fruit has obviously inspired the techs at Sigma, but Apple don’t short change on UI and this camera is somewhat clunky in this regard.

There’s being minimal and then there’s simply not delivering a full set of features for the sake of a limited UI.

For starters, if Apple made a camera, it would probably only have a large edge to edge touchscreen (with a very expensive optional detachable EVF)… it would probably work with ear buds for video and would also likely have a shutter button for the purists.

It would be running their M series processors as well, which would mean (in tandem with an obvious global or stacked shutter) could run insane fos at a high megapixel count.

They also wouldn’t price it anywhere near as cheaply as this, because every celeb and star around the planet would want one… and even Leica users would probably switch.

Author: @marslensart
Content:
This is one of the worst looking cameras I've seen and I've used A LOT of cameras. It's literally just a slab of aluminium with a lens on it. No charm, no personality, just bare metal. The ergonomics look like shit, if I took this on a multi-hour shoot I'd get tired of it digging into my hands. In fact, the first place I'd take this to shoot would be the recycling plant, because that's where these are going to end up.

This is a camera for tech bros, not for people who are serious about their craft.

No media card, no viewfinder, screen stays in place, buttons are basically unusable because there are so few of them leaving you with no room for customization.

Now you may say that "it's just for hobbyists! Not for professionals!" If that was the case then they wouldn't have made it cost the same as a used car on facebook marketplace. The internals are great, don't get me wrong, but if they cared about this being pushed to a demographic of professionals they wouldn't have made it look like a digicam with a lens on the front. Most people who care about photography and filmmaking don't want this kind of simplicity. If you buy this for the simplicity of its design, just use your phone.
